title: The woodpecker and the lion
hookLine: a woodpecker frees a bone from a lion's throat; the lion won't share (Jataka 308)

lines: A BONE IN A LION'S THROAT.
cards: A lion lies in the forest and can't eat. While he was gulping down his kill, a bone lodged in his throat, and now it's swelling and the pain won't stop.
A woodpecker on a branch above sees him suffering and flutters down to ask what's wrong. What is a bird supposed to do about a lion's throat? In the Javasakuna Jataka, quite a lot.

teach.h: A STICK PROPS THE JAWS OPEN.
teach.b: First, the stick. The woodpecker wants to help, but he isn't careless about it. A lion's mouth is no place to be.

So he props the lion's jaws wide open with a stick, goes in, knocks the bone loose with his beak, comes back out and knocks the stick away. Second, the hungry day. Some time later the woodpecker can find nothing to eat.

teach.h: THE BIRD ASKS FOR A SHARE.
teach.b: He comes across the lion feasting on a fresh kill, and asks, politely, for a little share. Third, the lion's answer. No.
You've been inside a lion's mouth, the lion says, and come out alive. Let that be payment enough. Fourth, what the bird does next.
A tree spirit living nearby asks the woodpecker why he doesn't strike back. He could peck at the lion's eyes. The woodpecker says no.
Nothing good comes of harming someone who doesn't know what he owes. He'll simply go.
And he flies off. A few days back, the elephant was good to a man who repaid him with a saw.
This tale asks a smaller, everyday question: what about help that's just never thanked? The woodpecker shows two things. Help wisely, with a stick in the jaws, so your kindness doesn't get you eaten.
And don't turn the help into a bill. He's still hungry when he flies away, and still free.

how: The Anguttara Nikaya names two kinds of people hard to find in the world: one who does a kindness first, and one who is grateful for it. In this tale the woodpecker is the first, and the lion is not the second.

o: ask again for what you're owed
pay back a harm with a harm

games.q: the woodpecker's tale: tap the pairs.
p: asked why the bird didn't strike back

s: the woodpecker climbed straight into the lion's open mouth
first he propped the jaws open with a stick.
the lion said surviving his mouth was payment enough
you've been inside a lion's mouth and lived, he says. be content.
the woodpecker pecked the lion's eyes in revenge
he refused, and simply flew away.

games.q: you're the woodpecker. you're hungry, and the lion you saved won't share a scrap. what do you do?
o: peck at his eyes while he eats.
tell every bird in the forest what he did.
games.why: the woodpecker sees no good in harming someone who doesn't know what he owes, so he simply leaves.

practice: Choose someone who could use a hand, and find your stick: the one sensible precaution, a set time, a clear limit, a question asked first, that keeps the help from costing more than you can give.
Then, before you've done anything, close the account in advance: no thanks expected, no share owed. Breathe with that.

wordCard.voice: Strike back. What the woodpecker wouldn't do to the lion who wouldn't share his meal, after freeing a bone from its throat, choosing instead to simply fly off. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: help anyway. Once it's given, it's given, and the bird flies off free. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya, Book of the Twos (two persons hard to find)
